extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, peer reviewers, and authors preparing or appraising narrative (non-systematic) review articles in medicine
extracted.subtask_description: Use the SANRA scale to evaluate the methodological and reporting quality of narrative (non-systematic) review articles in medical journals. The scale is a brief six-item instrument intended for editors, reviewers, and authors to support everyday editorial decisions and manuscript preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation of the review's importance (Item 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the manuscript explains the importance of the review topic—why the review matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0 (low) to 2 (high) with anchor definitions and examples provided in the SANRA 'explanations and instructions' document. Raters in the study often disagreed on this item; rater training and use of the anchor definitions are recommended to improve reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of the aims of the review (Item 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the review clearly states its aims or objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0–2 with anchor definitions and examples in the accompanying instructions. Item medians tended to be 1 in the study; use the provided anchors and training to standardize ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the literature search (Item 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether and how the manuscript describes the literature search methods (even for non-systematic reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0–2 with anchor examples in the instructions. In the field test this item had one of the lower mean scores and a lower item-total correlation (0.33), indicating variability; anchors and training should be used to guide consistent assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing (Item 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the adequacy, appropriateness and correctness of referencing and citation practices in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0–2 with anchor definitions and examples provided. Raters frequently disagreed on this item in the study, so careful application of the anchors and rater training (including group sessions) is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific reasoning / presentation of evidence level (Item 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the scientific reasoning, including presentation and appraisal of evidence levels within the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0–2 with anchor definitions and examples in the instructions document. The item is intended to capture how well the review presents and reasons about the evidence; apply the anchors to distinguish between low, intermediate, and high standards of reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of relevant and appropriate endpoint data (Item 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the review presents relevant and appropriate endpoint/outcome data pertinent to the review question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rated 0–2 with anchor examples in the accompanying document. Item showed higher item-total correlation in testing; use the anchors to judge completeness and appropriateness of presented endpoint data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring system and sum score
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the six items is rated in integers 0 (low standard), 1 (intermediate), or 2 (high standard); the maximal sum score is 12 and the sum score is intended to measure the construct 'quality of a narrative review article.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor definitions and examples guide item scoring (available in the SANRA explanations and instructions document). The scale is intentionally brief for day-to-day editorial use. No universally established cut-offs exist, but the authors' experience suggests a score of 4 or below indicates very poor quality. SANRA sum scores showed a modest association with editorial acceptance in one study; the authors recommend using SANRA as one decision aid among others (topic relevance, originality, journal-specific criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation and use guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendations for who should use SANRA and how to implement it in editorial/review workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended users: editors, reviewers, readers, and authors. The scale is feasible for routine editorial work but users should be trained using the supplied 'explanations and instructions' document; group training sessions are suggested. SANRA may complement journal-specific evaluations but should not replace consideration of other factors (audience, originality, difficulty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations, reliability, and validity notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychometric and practical limitations identified during development and testing of SANRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field test results: Cronbach's alpha = 0.68 (internal consistency), corrected item-total correlations 0.33–0.58, intra-class correlation coefficient (average measure) = 0.77 (95% CI 0.57–0.88) indicating acceptable inter-rater reliability but with lower confidence bound that may be unacceptable in some applications. Sample for testing was 30 manuscripts; authors advise further field testing (particularly validity) and emphasize rater training. Because SANRA is short (6 items) it does not cover all quality facets; users should not compare scores across different settings without caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded or de-emphasized domains (deleted/omitted items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domains explicitly not covered by SANRA or removed during revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors removed an item on the manuscript's writing and accessibility due to poor inter-rater reliability. SANRA does not cover some other important domains such as originality of the manuscript, and quality of tables and figures; these are acknowledged as important but intentionally excluded to keep the instrument brief. Users should consider these aspects separately when making editorial decisions.
